title: LeNet – The First CNN That Started It All
description: Exploring LeNet, one of the earliest convolutional neural networks that laid the foundation for modern deep learning.

body.raw: ## Context & Motivation When I think about where to start with convolutional neural networks (CNNs), it feels natural to begin with LeNet. This was the first real CNN that worked, built by Yann LeCun back in the 1990s and introduced in the paper *Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition*. And honestly, it’s also the first model I ever saw in a class when we switched from fully connected networks to image tasks. So it holds a bit of a “first step” feeling for me. At that time, people were trying to get computers to recognize handwritten digits, like the numbers on checks or zip codes on letters. The common approach was to design features by hand. These features included things like edge detectors, strokes, or corners. But handwriting is messy. People slant their digits, change the size, write quickly or slowly. Hand-crafted features just couldn’t handle all that variation. LeNet’s big idea was: what if the network *learns* those features directly from pixels? No manual feature engineering. Just raw 28×28 images of digits from the MNIST dataset, and let the network figure out edges, curves, and shapes on its own. That feels obvious to us now, but back then it was a huge shift. What surprised me when I first revisited this paper is how much of today’s CNN structure was already there: convolution layers to detect patterns, pooling to downsample, and fully connected layers at the end to do the classification. Even though the network looks tiny compared to models we use now, the blueprint was basically the same. So in this post, I want to walk through LeNet step by step. I’ll break down the architecture layer by layer, explain why they made the choices they did, and also show some PyTorch code for it. My hope is that if you’ve never seen a CNN before, this will feel like a clear and approachable first example. ## Architecture Breakdown Here’s where LeNet gets interesting. It might look small, but it’s built from the same building blocks that modern CNNs still use today. Think of it as the blueprint. ### Input The network takes in a 32×32 grayscale image. MNIST digits are 28×28, so the authors padded them to 32×32. Nothing fancy here, just making the math easier. ### First Convolution (C1) The first layer applies 6 filters of size 5×5. Each filter is like a stencil sliding over the image, picking out edges or curves. You end up with 6 new images (feature maps) that highlight different patterns. ### First Pooling (S2) Then comes average pooling. Imagine squinting at the image so small details blur out, but the big shapes stay visible. This reduces the size from 28×28 to 14×14. ### Second Convolution (C3) Now 16 new filters scan these smaller maps. This time the filters look for more complex shapes, like combinations of edges forming corners or loops. ### Second Pooling (S4) Another average pooling step, shrinking things down again. At this point the network is no longer staring at pixels, it’s staring at patterns of strokes and shapes. ### Third Convolution (C5) This layer uses 120 filters that cover the entire 5×5 maps. Each filter basically compresses a whole map into one number. Think of it as summarizing everything it’s seen so far into a set of key signals. ### Fully Connected (F6) and Output Finally, the model uses two fully connected layers. The first has 84 neurons, the second has 10 outputs (digits 0–9). This part is like a traditional neural network classifier, taking all the learned features and turning them into a prediction. --- Two things stand out: 1. Pooling was average pooling, not max pooling. Max pooling came later and is now more common. 2. Activations were tanh, not ReLU. ReLU was introduced much later with AlexNet in 2012. Even though LeNet is tiny compared to modern CNNs, the pattern is the same: convolution → pooling → convolution → pooling → fully connected → output. Once you understand this, bigger models like AlexNet and VGG make a lot more sense — they just add depth and scale. ## Implementation Notes To get a better feel for LeNet, I coded it out in PyTorch. Here’s a simplified version: ```python import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class LeNet5(nn.Module): def __init__(self): super(LeNet5, self).__init__() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(1, 6, kernel_size=5) # C1 self.pool1 = nn.AvgPool2d(2, stride=2) # S2 self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(6, 16, kernel_size=5) # C3 self.pool2 = nn.AvgPool2d(2, stride=2) # S4 self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(16, 120, kernel_size=5) # C5 self.fc1 = nn.Linear(120, 84) # F6 self.fc2 = nn.Linear(84, 10) # Output def forward(self, x): x = torch.tanh(self.conv1(x)) x = self.pool1(x) x = torch.tanh(self.conv2(x)) x = self.pool2(x) x = torch.tanh(self.conv3(x)) x = x.view(-1, 120) x = torch.tanh(self.fc1(x)) x = self.fc2(x) return x ``` I used tanh activations and average pooling to stay close to the original design. Out of curiosity, I tried swapping them for ReLU and max pooling, and the model performed better. That small test shows how later innovations didn’t reinvent CNNs, they just refined the same blueprint. Training this model on MNIST was fast and straightforward. On my machine it takes seconds, but it’s crazy to think that back in the 90s this was pushing the limits of compute. What feels like a toy model today was once cutting-edge. ## Why the Design Choices Matter One of the things I like about LeNet is that you can actually see the reasoning behind each design choice. **Convolutions over fully connected layers** If you tried to use a fully connected layer on a 32×32 image, you’d end up with thousands of weights right away. Convolutions solve that by reusing the same small filter everywhere, which keeps parameters manageable and also makes the network look for patterns across the whole image. **Pooling layers** Pooling is like zooming out. You lose a little detail but gain robustness. A digit shifted by a pixel or two still looks like the same digit after pooling, which helps with invariance. **Tanh activations** Today, we almost always use ReLU, but back then tanh was the standard. It squashes values into the range [-1, 1], which made optimization easier with the tools they had at the time. It’s slower than ReLU, but it got the job done. **Average pooling vs max pooling** LeNet used average pooling, which smooths things out. Nowadays max pooling is more common since it keeps the strongest signal. My guess is that average pooling felt more stable in the 90s, and computation was a big factor too. --- Seeing these choices in context makes me realize that nothing about modern CNNs is “magical.” The ideas were already here — we just changed the details as hardware and training methods improved. ## Reflections ## Reflections and What Came Next LeNet might look small today, but it showed me how powerful CNNs really are. Convolutions to find edges, pooling to simplify, and fully connected layers to make the final call — that recipe is still everywhere. What I found surprising is how many choices were different from what we’d use now. Tanh instead of ReLU, average pooling instead of max pooling. When I swapped those in my own code, training felt faster and accuracy improved. It made me realize later models weren’t doing something entirely new, just refining LeNet’s blueprint. And that blueprint carried forward. AlexNet scaled it up with GPUs and ReLU. VGG went deeper. GoogLeNet made it efficient. ResNet added skip connections. If you squint, they all still look like LeNet. That’s why this model feels like the “hello world” of CNNs — simple, but it gives you the mental map to understand everything that came after.
